query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys for high-temperature applications, a controlled reduction in elements that form non-protective oxides (e.g., Mn) and an enrichment in refractory oxide-forming elements (e.g., Cr and Ta) leads to the preferential formation of a dense, adherent, spinel-type oxide (e.g., CrTaO4-based) via sluggish diffusion, which in turn confers improved oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic high-entropy alloy containing multiple elements including Mn, Cr, Ta, Fe, Co, and Ni that in its standard composition tends to form non-protective Mn-rich oxides at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition to reduce the relative Mn content while enriching refractory elements such as Cr and Ta, to promote the formation of a stable, protective oxide phase.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high temperature conditions (e.g., 1000–1100 °C) in a controlled oxygen environment with constant oxygen partial pressure and prolonged exposure (e.g., up to 200 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, coherent, spinel-type oxide layer (e.g., CrTaO4-based oxide) that acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
generation.mechanism: The hypothesis postulates that reducing the concentration of Mn, which otherwise forms less protective, porous oxides, minimizes the depletion of bulk alloy components and encourages the preferential nucleation and growth of a refractory-element derived oxide. The inherent sluggish diffusion in HEAs limits rapid elemental migration, thereby stabilizing composition near the surface and aiding in the self-healing formation of a protective oxide film.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA will show a lower overall oxidation rate, demonstrated by reduced mass gain and the formation of a uniform, adherent, and protective CrTaO4-like spinel oxide layer, compared to the baseline HEA with higher Mn content.
generation.baseline: The original equiatomic HEA composition where higher Mn content leads predominantly to the formation of non-protective, Mn-rich oxides that result in higher oxidation rates and surface degradation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate under high-temperature, oxygen-rich conditions; deviations in temperature, environmental oxygen partial pressure, or exposure duration may alter the oxide formation kinetics and morphology.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether the same mechanistic pathway applies universally across all HEA systems, particularly given conflicting observations in systems where Mn dominates oxide formation (as seen in some studies) versus those enriched in refractory elements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with the standard equiatomic composition and one where the Mn content is reduced and compensated by increased amounts of Cr and Ta. Expose both samples to high temperature (1000–1100 °C) in a controlled oxygen environment for up to 200 hours. Use in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to measure oxide phase formation, layer morphology, and oxidation kinetics.
measurements: Phase identification and crystallography of the formed oxide layer (via in situ XRD)
Oxide layer thickness and adherence (via TEM)
Surface composition mapping (using techniques such as energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified HEA with reduced Mn content does not form a uniform, dense, and adherent CrTaO4-type or similarly protective spinel oxide layer, and if its oxidation rate is not significantly lower than that of the baseline HEA, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. ## Abstract
Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. ## Abstract
AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date.
